item.title: Jio IPO falls short of record payday for bankers despite mega issue
item.description: Jio Platforms is paying 19 banks about ₹196 crore in fees for its $3.1 billion IPO, just 0.65% of the issue size, as fierce competition squeezes investment banking earnings.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Jio Platforms raised a record amount of funds for billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s digital and telecommunications giant, but it proved to be far less lucrative for the bankers handling the deal. The company is paying about ₹196 crore ($20.7 million) in fees to the 19 banks on the roughly $3.1 billion IPO, according to filings. That amounts to about 0.65 per cent of the issue size, trailing the fee pools of several previous offerings in India. Fierce competition among investment bankers in India has compressed fees, particularly for marquee deals. Firms are often willing to accept thinner economics for a coveted role on high-profile transactions. The payoff can instead come through league-table rankings, bragging rights and credentials that help win the next big pitch. That’s a far cry from the days when Hyundai Motor India paid about ₹490 crore to bankers for its then-record ₹27,800 crore IPO in 2024. Paytm parent One 97 Communications paid about ₹320 crore for its ₹18,300 crore offering in 2021, while Swiggy Ltd handed out about ₹280 crore for its ₹11,300 crore share sale. Those types of windfalls have been elusive of late. National Stock Exchange of India, another blockbuster IPO this year, paid about ₹190 crore to a syndicate of 20 banks that worked on its roughly $2.4 billion offering, equivalent to about 0.8 per cent of the issue size. Bankers split fees of just ₹4.63 crore for SBI Funds Management of India’s billion-dollar offering in July. Investor enthusiasm, meanwhile, has been anything but restrained. Jio’s IPO was fully subscribed within the first 100 minutes of bidding and had attracted bids for nearly 22 times the shares on offer by Friday, according to BSE data.

item.title: News publishers contest new privacy law, fear impact on investigations
item.description: News publishers argue the law could threaten investigative journalism, expose confidential sources and force the removal of factual reports ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / India News / News publishers contest new privacy law, fear impact on investigations

News publishers contest new privacy law, fear impact on investigations News publishers argue the law could threaten investigative journalism, expose confidential sources and force the removal of factual reports

Supreme Court of India

Reuters New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 11:05 PM IST

Listen to This Article

A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged India's privacy law in court, arguing it would trample investigative work and let New Delhi identify journalists' sources, documents show. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government last year announced implementation of a privacy law to protect digital personal data of users, raising compliance requirements for platforms like Meta and Google. The publishers have said that since media outlets were not exempt, the law was an invasion of press freedom. Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written carve-out for journalists like in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, India's Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said in a confidential filing at the Supreme Court, reviewed by Reuters.

The October 6 lawsuit, being reported for the first time and due to be heard on Tuesday, is the most high-profile challenge to Modi's privacy law. Until now, only free speech activists and a group of smaller news outlets had challenged it. It also marks an unusual challenge to the government from businesses headed by Ambani and Adani, who opposition parties allege are close to Modi and get favourable treatment - charges the businesses and the government vehemently deny. Also Read

Can the CEC face prosecution? What the law says on accountability, immunity

BCI chairman Manan Kumar Mishra apologises to law students over NALSAR row

Govt tells Meta to ensure strict adherence to Indian law, content rules

Can an FIR simply be withdrawn? Why Neet protest cases may take time

NYT files motion to quash DOJ subpoenas over Air Force One coverage

DNPA and the media groups did not respond to requests for comment from Reuters, and neither did India's information technology ministry. The publishers are demanding that most of the law's contentious provisions, which kick in from May 2027, should be quashed. They are arguing the law could force a journalist to get prior consent from a person they want to investigate and force publishers to erase stories. They also say powers granted by the law to demand information could expose reporters' sources.

The law would "render investigative journalism a benign and neutered recorder of events," the 698-page filing said. The provisions "constitute pre-censorship which is anathema to any democracy worth its name". The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Modi took office in 2014. Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise Modi's government. India's ranking in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index fell to 157th out of 180 countries this year, from 140th in 2014 - but the government rejects the rankings. Modi's government says it respects press freedom and says India, which has a "vibrant press and media ecosystem" of hundreds of newspapers and TV channels, does not need validation from foreign bodies.

Concerns over consent   DNPA's members include Ambani's Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani's NDTV and other marquee media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India's largest-selling English-language daily. A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, the group's filing says. A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent "would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses". The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report.

Fear of sources at risk News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for non-compliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the "interests of the general public", which would curtail press freedom, DNPA said. In an August letter to the government attached to the lawsuit, the group said India "has chosen to grant broad exemptions to the state, while failing to extend any corresponding protection to the press". No response was cited. From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organization handling personal data "to furnish such information as it may call for", putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said.

It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued. The "nakedly unguided" provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power "can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant." (Reporting by Aditya Kalra)

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Meta eyes record $95 billion equity raise to fund AI infrastructure push
item.description: Meta plans $35 billion in stock offerings and a further $60 billion share sale programme to finance AI expansion, as heavy infrastructure spending strains its free cash flow ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Meta eyes record $95 billion equity raise to fund AI infrastructure push

Meta eyes record $95 billion equity raise to fund AI infrastructure push Meta plans $35 billion in stock offerings and a further $60 billion share sale programme to finance AI expansion, as heavy infrastructure spending strains its free cash flow

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 9:42 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Meta Platforms said on Monday it plans to raise up to $95 billion in its largest-ever equity fundraising, as the social media giant spends heavily on its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expansion.   The Facebook parent has launched public offerings worth about $35 billion in common and preferred stock and said it also plans to launch a separate at-the-market share sale programme worth up to $60 billion.   The company will launch the larger share sale programme after its new non-voting Class C shares begin trading, which is expected in the first quarter of 2027, but said it has not yet finalised the timing and terms of the sale.

Meta's fundraising plan, among the biggest by an AI company, has also drawn interest of up to $5 billion in total from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom for Class A shares.   Their funding interest adds to concerns about an increasingly circular flow of capital in the AI industry, as chip suppliers help finance the expansion of one of their biggest customers. Also Read

Zuckerberg strikes Meta deal to cover potential California billionaire tax

Meta's $25 bn penalty marks a massive win for New Mexico's attorney general

US court orders Meta to pay $25 bn for misleading users on data privacy

Australian govt to sue Facebook, TikTok for alleged breaches of ban

Govt asks Meta to avoid algorithmic bias towards limited set of narratives

Meta has been pouring money into chips and data centres to compete better with OpenAI and Anthropic.   "We expect investors to continue to question the financing and potential for future capital raises," William Blair analysts said in a note.   "Overall, we believe the financing reinforces both Meta's confidence in the long-term returns from AI investment and the increasingly capital-intensive nature of pursuing that opportunity."

The company's shares fell about 1.4 per cent in morning trading.   The latest fundraising further underscores a shift among big technology companies increasingly tapping debt markets and raising equity to bolster their AI infrastructure, having previously relied on cash to fund their investments.   Earlier this year, Alphabet increased the size of its equity offerings to $84.75 billion.   Separately on Monday, SpaceX said an affiliate of Apollo Global Management will buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them to the rockets-to-AI firm, in a deal with total principal payments of about $40 billion.   META'S AI SPENDING IS BURNING CASH   Meta has committed to spending about $825 billion in the future, primarily driven by its growing investments in data centres, AI-related infrastructure and cloud computing power.

But the rapid expansion has eroded its historically strong free cash flow.   The company reported a $2.12 billion cash burn in the third quarter, its first negative free cash flow in over a decade, compared with a positive cash flow of $10.63 billion a year ago.   Still, the early popularity of its consumer-focused AI agent Muse and the release of a competitive new series of AI models have helped partly justify Meta's substantial investments.   "We believe that Meta will ultimately produce a profitable AI business and its returns longer-term should help the company diversify, although the path may not be linear," William Blair analysts said.

The company had cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $82.45 billion and long-term debt of $80.92 billion as of September 30, according to its latest quarterly filing.   Last week, Meta raised the lower end of its annual capital expenditure forecast to a range of $135 billion to $145 billion.   The company has said it would issue Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively resulting in a two-for-one split, to fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control.   Meta agreed to grant Zuckerberg Class C shares that he can sell to help pay a potential California billionaire wealth tax, in exchange for a commitment to keep him in California.

item.description: MD and CEO Tarun Garg said the target is a baseline rather than a ceiling, as Hyundai expects the Creta and Bayon to appeal to different sets of mid-size SUV buyers ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Auto / Hyundai targets 250,000 mid-size SUV sales in 2027 on Creta, Bayon push

Hyundai targets 250,000 mid-size SUV sales in 2027 on Creta, Bayon push MD and CEO Tarun Garg said the target is a baseline rather than a ceiling, as Hyundai expects the Creta and Bayon to appeal to different sets of mid-size SUV buyers

Hyundai Motor India’s MD & CEO Tarun Garg said with Creta the firm is drawing on its brand value, while Bayon is aimed at buyers seeking a more tech-led experience

Deepak Patel New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 11:35 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Hyundai Motor India Ltd (HMIL) is expecting sales of at least 250,000 units of mid-size sport utility vehicles (SUVs) -- which include Creta and newly launched Bayon -- in 2027 due to rapid growth being observed in the segment for past several years and the two models’ ability to attract different sets of buyers, its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Tarun Garg said on Monday.   While speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the launch of the Bayon in Gurugram, Garg said the aforementioned target was a baseline rather than a ceiling. Bayon's deliveries are expected to begin during the ongoing festival season.     Garg said HMIL expects to sell around 170,000 units of the Creta in 2026. “The mid-SUV segment today is 16.5 per cent of the market already," he noted. The mid-size SUV segment in India has grown at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 25.6 per cent over the past five years and is projected to record 64 per cent volume growth between calendar years 2026 and 2032.   He said the segment’s size and growth made room for more than one model from the same manufacturer. Hyundai is now looking to build on the Creta’s established customer base through the Bayon.   The Bayon is being positioned differently from the Creta, with Hyundai targeting customers who are quicker to adopt new technology. Garg added that the distinction was based on customers’ attitudes and preferences rather than age, with the Creta drawing on its established brand value and loyal customer base, while the Bayon is aimed at buyers seeking a more technology-led experience. Also Read

Hyundai targets annual sales of 250,000 units from new Bayon, Creta

Car inventory levels lower this festival season amid rising demand premium

Hyundai Motor group to invest $15.5 billion in India over 7 years

Hyundai replicating India learnings across global markets: CEO Jose Muñoz

Hyundai Motor India sales rise 10.8% YoY to record 77,916 units in Sep

“Creta created a market (of mid-SUV segment) when it was launched 10 years. We expect that the launch of Bayon will allow us to do for next 10 years what Creta did then,” he stated.   Garg said Hyundai’s market research suggested petrol would account for the largest share of demand in the Bayon’s segment. The model will also get a compressed natural gas (CNG) option in January 2027. The company has not opted for a diesel version, as offering too many powertrain choices could complicate the product range and confuse buyers, he explained.   He also said user data generated through the Bayon’s artificial intelligence (AI)-powered voice assistant would remain with Hyundai and would not be shared with Perplexity, whose technology powers the underlying language model. SoundHound AI provides the voice technology and works with Hyundai globally.   Garg said Hyundai follows data privacy and security standards used in the United States and South Korea, where regulations are more developed than in India. “While some of these laws have not come to India, but they have been there in the US and Korea, much, much stronger," he stated.   Garg said Hyundai would continue selling the Verna despite the shrinking sedan market, as exports make the model viable. Verna was the company’s largest exported car, with domestic sales of around 7,000–10,000 units annually rising to 40,000–50,000 units when exports were included, he added.   “Verna has a very very important role in our portfolio. And we intend to continue with it even though the segment is de-growing,” he noted.   Hyundai plans to begin exporting the Bayon two to six months after its domestic launch, following its usual product-export strategy. Garg said the company would announce export destinations in due course. The SUV will be manufactured at Hyundai’s Chennai plant and is intended for more than 50 markets globally.   Garg also clarified that Hyundai Motor India’s $5 billion investment plan for 2025–2030 and Hyundai Motor Group’s $15.5 billion commitment for 2026–2032 have overlapping periods. He said spending planned for 2025 would be adjusted against the group’s broader plan, with additional investment expected to flow into the Indian subsidiary.   The company expects automatic transmissions to account for around 25 per cent of Bayon sales, with a margin of two percentage points either way. Garg said automatic transmission penetration across Hyundai’s portfolio was around 24-26 per cent, with the share generally higher in larger models.
